title: Preces Annae. Furor Didonis
titleEn: Anna's Embassy and Dido's Snare — Aeneid IV.408–503
about: The poet turns to Dido as she watches the shore from her citadel, boiling with Trojan activity, and asks what she felt. Love, he says, drives mortal hearts to anything: she is forced to go back to tears and prayer and to bow her pride, so as to leave nothing untried before she dies. She sends her sister Anna to Aeneas with a message. The sails are calling for the wind, the sailors have garlanded their sterns. She could bear such a blow if she had foreseen it, but Anna, whom he alone used to honour and to whom he told his secrets, must go to the proud enemy. Dido never swore with the Greeks at Aulis against Troy, never sent a fleet to Pergamum, never disturbed Anchises' ashes; why will he not let her words into his hard ears? She no longer asks for the marriage he betrayed, nor that he give up Latium; she asks only for empty time, a rest for her frenzy, until fortune teaches her to grieve. This last favour, once granted, she will repay with her death. Anna carries the weeping to and fro, but Aeneas is not moved. The fates stand in the way and a god stops the hero's calm ears. Like an old oak on the Alps, tugged now from this side and now from that by the north winds, which groans and sheds its leaves but clings with its roots as deep in the underworld as its crown is high in the sky, he is battered on every side by pleas and feels the pain in his great heart, yet his mind stays fixed and his tears roll down to no purpose. Then Dido, terrified by her fate, begs for death and is tired of the sky. As she lays gifts on the incense altars, the holy water goes black and the poured wine turns into foul blood; she tells no one, not even her sister. In her palace stands a marble shrine of her first husband, which she tends with great reverence, hung with white fleeces and festive leaves; from it she seems to hear her husband's voice calling in the night, and an owl on the roof laments in a long death-song. The warnings of old seers terrify her. In dreams the savage Aeneas drives her on, and she is always alone, always walking a long road, looking for her Tyrians in a deserted land. She is like Pentheus raving, seeing the troops of the Furies and a double sun and a double Thebes; or like Orestes on the stage, fleeing his mother armed with torches and black snakes while the avenging Furies sit at the door. So, beaten by grief, she settles on death, works out the time and the manner, and goes to her sister with a calm face and a brow bright with false hope. She has found a way, she says, to bring Aeneas back or free her from loving him. At the edge of Ocean, where Atlas turns the star-studded heavens on his shoulder, a priestess of the Massylians, keeper of the Hesperides' temple, who feeds the dragon and guards the sacred boughs, has been pointed out to her; by spells she frees or binds minds, stops rivers, turns the stars back, and rouses the ghosts of the night. Dido swears by the gods and by Anna's life that she takes up magic unwillingly. Anna is to build a pyre secretly in the inner part of the house under the open sky and pile on it the arms the traitor left hanging in her chamber, all his spoils and the marriage bed where she was ruined, for she wishes to destroy every trace of the accursed man. She falls silent and goes pale. Anna does not suspect that the new rites cloak a funeral, nor imagine any greater madness than at the death of Sychaeus, and so she does as she is told.

sentences.t: Quis tibi tum, Dido, cernenti talia sensus?
sentences.l: What feeling to you then, Dido, seeing such things?
sentences.i: Dido, what passed through your heart then, as you beheld such things?
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. The poet speaks straight to his character (apostrophe), a device Virgil uses at moments of high pathos; you will meet it again. 'tibi' is a dative of possession with 'est' understood: 'what feeling was there to you', i.e. 'what did you feel'. 'cernenti' is a present participle in the dative, agreeing with 'tibi': 'to you seeing'. 'talia' is neuter plural, 'such things': the Trojan preparations described at the end of the last part.

sentences.t:
quosve dabas gemitus, cum litora fervere late
prospiceres arce ex summa, totumque videres
misceri ante oculos tantis clamoribus aequor?
sentences.l:
Or what groans were you giving, when the shores to seethe far and wide
you looked out upon from the topmost citadel, and the whole you saw
to be churned together before your eyes with such great shouts, the sea?
sentences.i: What groans did you utter when, from the height of your citadel, you saw the shores boiling with activity far and wide, and the whole sea in turmoil before your eyes with such an uproar?
sentences.n: 'quosve': '-ve' is an enclitic meaning 'or'. 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctives 'prospiceres' and 'videres' gives the circumstance, addressed to Dido in the second person. 'litora fervere' and 'totum… aequor misceri' are accusatives and infinitives after the verbs of seeing; 'fervere' recalls the ants' path in the simile just before, which 'fervet' (407). 'totum' and 'aequor' stand at opposite ends of the clause, enclosing it. 'arce ex summa' puts the preposition between noun and adjective. 'clamoribus' is an ablative of cause or means.

sentences.t: Improbe Amor, quid non mortalia pectora cogis?
sentences.l: Shameless Love, what do you not force mortal hearts to?
sentences.i: Ruthless Love, what is there that you do not force mortal hearts to do?
sentences.n: 'Improbe' is a vocative: another apostrophe, now to the god Amor (Love). The adjective means 'shameless, wicked' and, of a force that does not let up, 'relentless': 'shameless' in the literal line, 'ruthless' in the English. 'quid non' is an idiom: 'what do you not (compel them to do)'. 'cogis' takes the accusative 'pectora' and a neuter 'quid' as an accusative of what they are driven to. 'mortalia pectora' is a neuter plural: 'hearts' for 'people'.

sentences.t:
Ire iterum in lacrimas, iterum temptare precando
cogitur, et supplex animos submittere amori,
ne quid inexpertum frustra moritura relinquat.
sentences.l:
To go again into tears, again to try by praying
she is forced, and as a suppliant to bow her spirit to love,
lest anything untried, in vain about to die, she leave behind.
sentences.i: She is driven to go once more into tears, once more to try what prayer can do, and as a suppliant to humble her pride before love, so that she may leave nothing untried and not die in vain.
sentences.n: 'cogitur' is the passive of 'cogo', and three infinitives depend on it: 'ire', 'temptare', 'submittere'. The repeated 'iterum' is anaphora. 'precando' is the ablative of the gerund of the deponent 'precor', 'by praying'. 'supplex' is a predicate adjective, 'as a suppliant'. 'submittere… amori' takes the dative. 'ne quid… relinquat' is a negative purpose clause (present subjunctive; 'quid' is the indefinite after 'ne'). 'moritura' is the future participle of 'morior', 'about to die', and 'frustra' is probably taken with it: she must not die having left something untried. The Latin Library's 'summittere' is the same word with different spelling.

sentences.t: “Anna, vides toto properari litore;
sentences.l: “Anna, you see it to be hurried on the whole shore;
sentences.i: “Anna, you see how they hurry along the whole shore;
sentences.n: Dido's speech to Anna opens here, so Greenough prints the opening quotation mark; it runs to 436, and this line begins a new paragraph. Anna is Dido's sister and confidante. 'properari' is an impersonal passive infinitive after 'vides': 'you see (that) there is hurrying', as Latin can make a passive of an intransitive verb. 'toto litore' is an ablative of place with no preposition, as is regular with 'totus'.

sentences.t:
circum
undique convenere;
sentences.l:
around
from everywhere they have gathered;
sentences.i: from every side they have gathered round;
sentences.n: 'circum' is an adverb here, 'around', and it closes line 416. 'convenere' is 'convenerunt', the perfect with the ending '-ere' for '-erunt'. You will see this constantly. The unnamed subject is the Trojans.

sentences.t:
vocat iam carbasus auras,
puppibus et laeti nautae imposuere coronas.
sentences.l:
now the canvas calls the breezes,
on the sterns and glad the sailors have placed garlands.
sentences.i: the sails are already beckoning the breezes, and the cheerful sailors have set garlands on the sterns.
sentences.n: 'carbasus' is a Greek loanword for fine linen, then a sail; it is the grammatical subject, 'the canvas calls'. 'puppibus' is a dative with the compound verb 'imposuere' (= 'imposuerunt'). 'et' joins this clause to the last and stands second in its own clause, after 'puppibus'. Garlands on the sterns suggest a departure at sea: the Trojans are cheerful, and Dido is looking on.

sentences.t:
Hunc ego si potui tantum sperare dolorem,
et perferre, soror, potero.
sentences.l:
This so great grief, if I was able to look forward to it,
and to bear it through, sister, I shall be able.
sentences.i: If I could foresee a grief as great as this, I shall be able to bear it to the end, sister.
sentences.n: 'si potui… potero': the condition is in the perfect and the main verb in the future: 'if I was able, I shall be able'. 'Hunc… tantum… dolorem' is one noun phrase, with 'tantum' an adjective in agreement, not the adverb; it is the object of both 'sperare' and 'perferre'. 'spero' can mean 'look forward to, expect', even of a dreaded thing. 'ego' is emphatic. 'soror' is a vocative.

sentences.t:
Miserae hoc tamen unum
exsequere, Anna, mihi.
sentences.l:
To wretched me this yet one thing
carry out, Anna, for me.
sentences.i: Yet do this one thing for me, wretched as I am, Anna.
sentences.n: 'miserae' is a dative agreeing with 'mihi' at the end of the sentence; it is put first, and 'mihi' repeats 'me' as an emotional 'for me'. 'miserae' is Dido's word for herself in this speech; it comes back at 429. 'hoc unum' is the object of 'exsequere', the imperative of the deponent 'exsequor', 'carry out'. 'tamen' means 'all the same': she says she will bear the blow, but still asks this.

sentences.t:
Solam nam perfidus ille
te colere, arcanos etiam tibi credere sensus;
sentences.l:
For you alone that faithless man
to cherish, even secret feelings to you to entrust;
sentences.i: For he, the faithless man, would show regard for you alone, and entrust his secret thoughts even to you;
sentences.n: 'colere' and 'credere' are historic infinitives: the infinitive used for a vivid imperfect, with its subject ('ille') in the nominative. You will meet this several times. 'Solam' agrees with 'te' and is put first for emphasis; 'nam' comes second in its clause. 'perfidus' is Dido's word for Aeneas. 'arcanos… sensus' is the object of 'credere', with 'tibi' the dative.

sentences.t: sola viri mollis aditus et tempora noras.
sentences.l: you alone the man's gentle approaches and the times knew.
sentences.i: You alone knew the gentle ways of approaching the man, and the right moments.
sentences.n: 'sola' is nominative, 'you alone', picking up 'solam' (the same word repeated). 'noras' is 'noveras', the pluperfect of 'nosco' with the contracted form, and it has the sense 'knew'. 'mollis' is '-is' for '-es', accusative plural, agreeing with 'aditus' (fourth declension, 'approaches'). 'viri' is Aeneas, 'the man'; Dido avoids his name here.

sentences.t: I, soror, atque hostem supplex adfare superbum:
sentences.l: Go, sister, and the enemy as a suppliant address, the proud one:
sentences.i: Go, sister, and speak to the proud enemy as a suppliant:
sentences.n: 'I' is the imperative of 'eo'. 'adfare' is the imperative of the deponent 'adfor', 'speak to', with an accusative object. 'hostem' is a bitter word for her lover. 'supplex' is a nominative, qualifying the subject, 'you as a suppliant'. The colon introduces the message Anna is to carry.

sentences.t:
non ego cum Danais Troianam exscindere gentem
Aulide iuravi, classemve ad Pergama misi,
nec patris Anchisae cineres Manisve revelli,
cur mea dicta neget duras demittere in auris.
sentences.l:
not I with the Danaans the Trojan to destroy race
at Aulis swore, or a fleet to Pergama sent,
nor of father Anchises the ashes or the Shades tore up,
why my words should he refuse into his hard ears to let.
sentences.i: I did not swear with the Greeks at Aulis to destroy the Trojan people, nor send a fleet against Pergamum, nor tear up the ashes or the shade of his father Anchises: why should he refuse to let my words into his hard ears?
sentences.n: She has done him no wrong, so why should he refuse? Aulis was the harbour where the Greeks gathered for Troy. 'iuravi' takes the infinitive 'exscindere'. 'Pergama' is neuter plural, Troy's citadel. 'Manisve': 'Manis' is '-is' for 'Manes', accusative plural, the spirits of the dead; 'revelli' is the perfect of 'revello' and governs both 'cineres' and 'Manis'. 'cur… neget' is a subjunctive in an indignant question, 'why should he refuse'; the Latin Library's 'negat' would ask the plain question, 'why does he refuse'. Its 'cinerem' (singular) at 427 changes nothing in sense.

sentences.t: Quo ruit?
sentences.l: Where does he rush?
sentences.i: Where is he rushing?
sentences.n: The message breaks off in a cry. 'ruit' is the present of 'ruo', 'rush headlong'; 'quo' is 'to what place'. Dido speaks of Aeneas in the third person throughout the message, as if he were not there.

sentences.t: Extremum hoc miserae det munus amanti:
sentences.l: This last gift, to the wretched woman in love, let him give:
sentences.i: Let him grant this last favour to a hapless woman who loves him:
sentences.n: 'det' is a present subjunctive used as a command, 'let him give' (third person, so it cannot be an imperative). 'Extremum hoc… munus' encloses the verb. 'miserae amanti' is a dative: 'amanti' is a present participle used as a noun, 'to the one loving', and 'miserae' agrees with it. The colon introduces what the gift is.

sentences.t: exspectet facilemque fugam ventosque ferentis.
sentences.l: let him wait for both an easy flight and winds that carry him.
sentences.i: let him wait for a smooth passage and for winds that will bear him on.
sentences.n: 'exspectet' is another jussive subjunctive; the subject is Aeneas, understood from 'Quo ruit?'. 'facilem' means 'easy', here a smooth, untroubled passage, and 'fugam' is Dido's word for his sailing, 'flight'. 'ferentis' is '-is' for '-es', accusative plural, present participle of 'fero' agreeing with 'ventos', 'winds that carry'. She asks for nothing but a wait until the weather is fair.

sentences.t:
Non iam coniugium antiquum, quod prodidit, oro,
nec pulchro ut Latio careat regnumque relinquat:
sentences.l:
Not now the marriage old, which he betrayed, do I ask,
nor that of fair Latium he go without and his kingdom abandon:
sentences.i: I no longer ask for the old marriage, which he betrayed, nor that he go without lovely Latium and give up his kingdom:
sentences.n: 'oro' governs the accusative 'coniugium', and then an 'ut' clause: 'nec… ut careat… relinquat' (present subjunctives), 'nor (do I ask) that he lack… and leave'. 'non iam' means 'no longer'. 'quod prodidit' is a relative clause, 'which he betrayed'. 'carere' takes the ablative ('Latio'). 'pulchro' may be bitter: she grants him his fair Italy. 'antiquum' means 'former, of old', as it does of Sychaeus at 458.

sentences.t:
tempus inane peto, requiem spatiumque furori,
dum mea me victam doceat fortuna dolere.
sentences.l:
time empty I ask, rest and space for frenzy,
until my fortune teach me, conquered, to grieve.
sentences.i: I ask for an empty stretch of time, a rest and a space for my frenzy, until fortune teaches me, beaten as I am, how to grieve.
sentences.n: 'tempus inane' is 'a blank time', time with nothing in it. 'furori' is a dative of advantage, 'for my frenzy'. 'dum' with a present subjunctive means 'until' with an aim: she is waiting for something she hopes will happen. 'doceat' takes the person taught, 'me victam', and the thing taught, the infinitive 'dolere' ('to grieve'); 'victam' agrees with 'me'. The theme of her being 'conquered' returns at 474 ('evicta').

sentences.t: Extremam hanc oro veniam—miserere sororis—
sentences.l: Last this I ask, a favour—pity your sister—
sentences.i: This is the last favour I ask—take pity on your sister—
sentences.n: The dashes enclose a parenthesis. The appeal 'miserere sororis' turns from the message for Aeneas to Anna herself: 'have pity on your sister'. 'miserere' is the imperative of the deponent 'misereor', which takes the genitive. 'veniam' is a favour or indulgence; 'Extremam hanc… veniam' frames the verb 'oro'.

sentences.t: quam mihi cum dederit, cumulatam morte remittam.”
sentences.l: which to me when he has granted, piled high with death I shall give back.”
sentences.i: once he has granted it to me, I shall give it back to him piled high with my death.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: Dido's speech to Anna ends here. 'quam' is a connecting relative (it refers to 'veniam'): 'which, when…'. 'cum dederit' is a future perfect: 'when he shall have given'. 'cumulatam' agrees with the understood object of 'remittam', 'heaped up'; 'morte' is an ablative of means. Dido's bargain hides her plan, and the hint is lost on Anna.

sentences.t:
Talibus orabat, talisque miserrima fletus
fertque refertque soror:
sentences.l:
With such words she begged, and such tears, most wretched,
both carries and carries back her sister:
sentences.i: Such were her pleas, and such the tears that her sister, in utmost misery, bore to him and bore back again:
sentences.n: 'Talibus' is an ablative, with 'verbis' understood. 'orabat' is the imperfect, 'she kept begging', and its subject 'soror' (Anna) is held to the end of the clause, with 'miserrima' (superlative, 'most wretched') in agreement. 'talisque… fletus' is the object; 'talis' is '-is' for '-es'. 'fertque refertque' is a double '-que' ('both… and') with 'fero' and its compound 'refero': she goes to and fro, bearing the tears.

sentences.t:
sed nullis ille movetur
fletibus, aut voces ullas tractabilis audit;
sentences.l:
but by no tears he is moved,
or any voices, pliable, does he hear;
sentences.i: but he is moved by none of these tears, nor does he lend a yielding ear to any word she says;
sentences.n: 'ille' is Aeneas, 'that man'. 'nullis… fletibus' is an ablative of means; 'aut' after a negative means 'nor'. 'ullas' is the 'any' that Latin uses after a negative. 'tractabilis' is an adjective where English prefers an adverb, 'yieldingly'; literally 'that can be handled, workable'.

sentences.t: fata obstant, placidasque viri deus obstruit auris.
sentences.l: the fates stand in the way, and the man's tranquil a god blocks ears.
sentences.i: the fates oppose her, and a god closes the hero's calm ears against her.
sentences.n: 'obstant' and 'obstruit' both begin with 'ob-', 'against': the first 'stand in the way', the second 'build against, block up'. 'fata' is a neuter plural, 'the fates', his destiny. 'deus' is left unnamed; the reader may think of the divine order Mercury brought. The line puts the cause in fate and a god, not in Aeneas's own hardness of heart. 'viri' is 'of the man' (Aeneas), 'placidas' means 'calm, untroubled', and 'auris' is '-is' for '-es', accusative plural.

sentences.i: As when northern gales from the Alps, battering now from this side and now from that, contend among themselves to tear up a sturdy oak, heavy with years;
sentences.n: The oak simile runs to 449; its main clause begins at 'haud secus' (447), 'not otherwise'. It is an epic simile: winds struggling over a tree. 'velut… cum' means 'just as when'. 'Alpini Boreae' is the plural subject: 'Boreae' is a nominative plural, the north winds. 'annoso… robore' is an ablative of description: 'robur' is oak-timber, the hard wood. 'eruere' here is an infinitive, 'to uproot', depending on 'certant' ('strive to'), and not the perfect '-ere'. 'inter se' means 'with each other'.

sentences.t:
it stridor, et altae
consternunt terram concusso stipite frondes;
sentences.l:
goes a shriek, and the lofty
strew the ground, the trunk being shaken, leaves;
sentences.i: a shrill roar goes up, and the tall foliage, as the trunk is shaken, strews the ground;
sentences.n: 'it' is the present of 'eo': 'a shriek goes (up)', as the ant column 'goes' at 404. 'stridor' is a third-declension noun (genitive 'stridoris'). 'concusso stipite' is an ablative absolute, 'the trunk having been shaken'. 'altae… frondes' ('the tall leaves') frames the rest of the clause. 'consternunt' is 'strew over'.

sentences.t:
ipsa haeret scopulis, et, quantum vertice ad auras
aetherias, tantum radice in Tartara tendit:
sentences.l:
itself it clings to the rocks, and, as far as with its crown to the airs
of the upper sky, so far with its root to Tartarus it stretches:
sentences.i: the tree itself clings to the rocks, and as far as its crown reaches up into the airs of heaven, so far its root stretches down to Tartarus:
sentences.n: 'ipsa' is the oak itself, as opposed to its leaves. 'haeret scopulis' is 'clings to the rocks' (the noun can be read as a dative after 'haereo' or as an ablative of place). 'quantum… tantum' is 'as far as… so far'. 'vertice' and 'radice' are ablatives, 'with its crown' and 'with its root'. 'Tartara' is a neuter plural: the lowest part of the underworld. Virgil had written almost these words of a tree in Georgics 2.

sentences.t:
haud secus adsiduis hinc atque hinc vocibus heros
tunditur, et magno persentit pectore curas;
sentences.l:
not otherwise with unceasing, from here and from there, words the hero
is battered, and in his great heart feels through the pangs;
sentences.i: just so is the hero battered by the unceasing pleas that come at him from this side and that, and he feels the pangs deep in his great heart;
sentences.n: 'haud secus' takes up 'velut' (441): the comparison turns to Aeneas. 'adsiduis' is Greenough's spelling of 'assiduis', 'unceasing'. 'hinc atque hinc' answers the winds' 'hinc… illinc'. 'heros' is a Greek nominative. 'tunditur' is 'is beaten', as the oak is. 'persentit' has intensive 'per-', 'feels thoroughly'. 'magno… pectore' is an ablative of place, 'in his great heart'. 'curas' can be his pangs or Dido's; Virgil does not say.

sentences.t: mens immota manet;
sentences.l: the mind unmoved remains;
sentences.i: his resolve stays unshaken;
sentences.n: The simile's point: the oak holds. 'mens' is will or purpose. 'immota' recalls 'immota… lumina' of his eyes in the last part (331). Three short words, with the alliteration of 'm'.

sentences.t: lacrimae volvuntur inanes.
sentences.l: tears roll, empty.
sentences.i: and tears fall to no purpose.
sentences.n: 'volvuntur' is passive in form with middle sense, 'roll'. 'inanes' means 'empty, fruitless'. The line does not say whose tears they are: Aeneas's own, or Anna's, or Dido's through Anna; the line leaves it open.

sentences.t:
Tum vero infelix fatis exterrita Dido
mortem orat;
sentences.l:
Then indeed unhappy, by the fates terrified, Dido
asks for death;
sentences.i: Then, truly, ill-starred Dido, terrified by her fate, prays for death;
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'Tum vero' marks the turn, 'then indeed'. 'infelix' means 'ill-starred', literally 'not fruitful, not lucky'. 'fatis' is an ablative of cause. 'exterrita' is a perfect passive participle, 'terrified' (it describes the state she is in). 'orat' is the present of 'oro', 'beg for', with the object 'mortem'. Her pleas to Aeneas ('orabat', 437) have given way to a prayer for death.

sentences.t: taedet caeli convexa tueri.
sentences.l: it wearies her the vaults of heaven to behold.
sentences.i: she is weary of gazing on the arching heavens.
sentences.n: 'taedet' is impersonal: 'it wearies (her)', with the person in the accusative, here understood, and an infinitive, 'tueri' (the deponent 'tueor', 'look at'). 'caeli convexa' is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun with a genitive: 'the vaults of the sky'.

sentences.t:
Quo magis inceptum peragat lucemque relinquat,
vidit, turicremis cum dona imponeret aris,
horrendum dictu, latices nigrescere sacros,
fusaque in obscenum se vertere vina cruorem.
sentences.l:
That the more her undertaking she carry through and leave the light,
she saw, when on the incense-burning altars she was placing gifts,
awful to tell, the holy waters to turn black,
and the poured wine into foul gore to change itself.
sentences.i: To make her the more set on finishing what she had begun and leaving the light, she saw, as she laid her offerings on the incense-burning altars, a horror to speak of: the holy water turning black, and the poured wine changing into foul blood.
sentences.n: 'Quo magis' with the subjunctives 'peragat' and 'relinquat' is a purpose clause containing a comparative: 'in order that the more…'. 'inceptum' is a neuter participle used as a noun, 'what she had begun'. 'lucem relinquat' means 'leave the light', to die. The main verb 'vidit' is held back, and 'cum… imponeret' is a circumstantial clause. 'turicremis' is a compound adjective (incense-burning) on 'aris' (dative with 'imponeret'). 'horrendum dictu' uses the supine in '-u', 'awful to tell'. 'latices' means 'liquids, waters' (plural of 'latex'). 'nigrescere' and 'se vertere' are infinitives after 'vidit'. 'obscenum' means 'foul, ill-omened'.

sentences.t: Hoc visum nulli, non ipsi effata sorori.
sentences.l: This sight to no one, not to her sister herself, having told.
sentences.i: This sight she told to no one, not even to her own sister.
sentences.n: 'visum' is the neuter participle of 'video' used as a noun, 'a sight'; it is the object of 'effata'. 'effata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'effor', and it has an active sense, 'having spoken'; the verb 'est' is understood. 'nulli' is a dative, 'to no one'. 'non ipsi… sorori' means 'not even to her sister herself'. Dido's concealment begins.

sentences.t:
Praeterea fuit in tectis de marmore templum
coniugis antiqui, miro quod honore colebat,
velleribus niveis et festa fronde revinctum:
sentences.l:
Besides there was in the palace a shrine of marble
of her husband of old, which with wondrous honour she tended,
with snowy fleeces and festal leaves wreathed about:
sentences.i: Besides, in her palace there stood a marble shrine to her husband of old, which she tended with wondrous reverence, bound about with snowy fleeces and festal foliage:
sentences.n: A second portent. 'tectis' (literally 'roofs') means 'the palace'; 'de marmore' goes with 'templum', 'a shrine of marble'. 'coniugis antiqui' is Sychaeus, her first husband, killed by her brother Pygmalion; 'antiqui' means 'former', as at 431. 'miro quod honore colebat' is a relative clause: the imperfect shows her habit. 'velleribus niveis' are snow-white fleeces (strips of wool), a ritual decoration; 'festa fronde' is 'festal foliage'. 'revinctum' is a perfect participle agreeing with 'templum'.

sentences.t:
hinc exaudiri voces et verba vocantis
visa viri, nox cum terras obscura teneret;
sentences.l:
from there to be heard voices and the words of one calling
seemed, of her husband, when night, dark, held the lands;
sentences.i: from it voices seemed to be heard, and the words of her husband calling to her, when dark night held the earth;
sentences.n: 'hinc' means 'from there', from the shrine. 'exaudiri' is a passive infinitive, 'to be heard (distinctly)'. 'visa' is short for 'visa sunt', 'seemed', a personal construction: 'voces et verba' are the subject and 'exaudiri' depends on 'visa'. 'vocantis viri' is 'of her calling husband'. 'cum… teneret' is an imperfect subjunctive of circumstance; 'obscura' agrees with 'nox', 'dark'. The voice she hears is her dead husband Sychaeus calling.

sentences.t:
solaque culminibus ferali carmine bubo
saepe queri et longas in fletum ducere voces;
sentences.l:
and alone on the roof-tops with a deadly song an owl
often to lament and long into weeping to draw out cries;
sentences.i: and often, alone on the rooftops, an owl would lament with its song of death and draw its long cries out into weeping;
sentences.n: 'queri' and 'ducere' are historic infinitives again, with their subject 'bubo', 'the owl', in the nominative (as 'colere' at 422). 'sola' agrees with 'bubo', 'solitary'. 'culminibus' is an ablative of place. 'ferali carmine' is an ablative of manner: 'ferale' means 'of death, funereal', and the owl was a bird of ill omen. 'in fletum ducere' means 'to draw out into a wail'.

sentences.t:
multaque praeterea vatum praedicta priorum
terribili monitu horrificant.
sentences.l:
and many besides, of seers, of earlier ones, the predictions
with dread warning make her shudder.
sentences.i: And many predictions of the seers of old, besides, fill her with dread by their fearful warning.
sentences.n: 'multa… praedicta' is the subject, 'many predictions', a neuter plural from the noun 'praedictum'. The genitive phrase 'vatum… priorum' ('of earlier seers') is split around 'praedicta'. 'terribili monitu' is an ablative of means, 'by terrible warning' (fourth declension). 'horrificant' is transitive; its object, 'her', is understood.

sentences.t:
Agit ipse furentem
in somnis ferus Aeneas;
sentences.l:
Drives, himself, her raging
in dreams fierce Aeneas;
sentences.i: In her dreams Aeneas himself, savage, drives her on in her frenzy;
sentences.n: 'agit' is 'drives, hounds', as in a hunt. 'furentem' is an accusative present participle agreeing with an understood 'eam', 'her raging'. 'ipse' is Aeneas in person, over against the portents. 'ferus' means 'wild, cruel': it is how the dream shows him, not necessarily the poet's verdict. 'in somnis' means 'in dreams'.

sentences.t:
semperque relinqui
sola sibi, semper longam incomitata videtur
ire viam, et Tyrios deserta quaerere terra.
sentences.l:
and always to be left
alone to herself, always a long, unaccompanied, she seems
to go road, and Tyrians to seek, in a deserted land.
sentences.i: She always seems to be left alone to herself, always seems to travel a long road with no companion, and to seek her Tyrians in a deserted land.
sentences.n: 'videtur' is a personal passive, 'she seems', with the infinitives 'relinqui', 'ire', 'quaerere'. 'sola sibi' means 'alone with herself'. 'incomitata' is 'unaccompanied'. 'longam… viam' frames 'incomitata videtur ire': the long road around her. 'Tyrios' are her own people. 'deserta' most naturally agrees with 'terra' ('a deserted land'), though it could also go with Dido ('forsaken').

sentences.t:
Eumenidum veluti demens videt agmina Pentheus,
et solem geminum et duplicis se ostendere Thebas;
sentences.l:
As of the Eumenides the bands, mad, sees Pentheus,
and a sun twofold and, double, to show themselves Thebes;
sentences.i: Just as raving Pentheus beholds the troops of the Furies, and sees a double sun, and two Thebes presenting themselves;
sentences.n: A double simile from Greek tragedy: Dido is like Pentheus or Orestes. Pentheus, king of Thebes, was driven mad for resisting Dionysus; in Euripides' Bacchae he sees two suns and a double Thebes. In Greek tragedy the Furies pursue Orestes, not Pentheus: Virgil joins the two madmen. 'Eumenidum' is a genitive plural in '-um' (the Furies, euphemistically 'the Kindly Ones'). 'veluti' means 'just as'. 'demens' means 'out of his mind'. 'duplicis' is '-is' for '-es'; the form 'Thebas' is a Greek plural name. 'videt' takes 'agmina' and 'solem' as objects and 'Thebas se ostendere' as an accusative and infinitive.

sentences.t:
aut Agamemnonius scaenis agitatus Orestes
armatam facibus matrem et serpentibus atris
cum fugit, ultricesque sedent in limine Dirae.
sentences.l:
or Agamemnon's son on the stage driven, Orestes,
her armed with torches mother and with serpents black
when he flees, and the avenging sit on the threshold Furies.
sentences.i: or as Agamemnon's son Orestes, driven on the stage, when he flees his mother armed with torches and black snakes, while the avenging Furies sit at the door.
sentences.n: 'Agamemnonius' is a patronymic adjective, 'son of Agamemnon'. Orestes killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge Agamemnon and was then hounded by her Furies (a story the Greek tragedians put on the stage). 'scaenis' is an ablative plural, 'on the stage', and shows Virgil has the theatre in mind. 'agitatus' is a perfect participle, 'driven'. 'armatam facibus… et serpentibus atris': 'armed' with torches and snakes, as a Fury. 'cum fugit' is the present, 'when he flees'. 'Dirae' is the Latin name for the Furies; 'ultrices' is 'avenging'.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi concepit furias evicta dolore
decrevitque mori, tempus secum ipsa modumque
exigit, et, maestam dictis adgressa sororem,
consilium voltu tegit, ac spem fronte serenat:
sentences.l:
So when she conceived frenzies, overcome by grief,
and decided to die, the time with herself, herself, and the manner
she works out, and, her sorrowing with words having approached sister,
her plan with her face she covers, and hope with her brow she brightens:
sentences.i: So when, overcome by grief, she had conceived her madness and resolved to die, she worked out in her own mind the time and the manner, and, going to her grieving sister with words, she hid her plan behind her face and put on a brow bright with hope:
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'ubi' with the perfect tenses 'concepit' and 'decrevit' means 'as soon as'. 'concepit furias' uses the verb of conceiving a child; 'evicta' is a perfect passive participle, 'utterly overcome', with 'dolore' an ablative of cause. 'decrevit' takes the infinitive 'mori'. 'adgressa' is a deponent perfect participle with active sense, 'having accosted'. 'voltu' is Greenough's form of 'vultu', 'face' (the Latin Library prints 'uultu', the same). 'consilium voltu tegit, spem fronte serenat' is a matched pair: the face hides the plan, the brow shines with false hope.

sentences.t:
“Inveni, germana, viam—gratare sorori—
quae mihi reddat eum, vel eo me solvat amantem.
sentences.l:
“I have found, sister, a way—congratulate your sister—
which to me may restore him, or from him release me, loving.
sentences.i: “Sister, I have found a way—wish your sister joy—that will either give him back to me or release me from loving him.
sentences.n: Dido's speech to Anna opens here, so Greenough prints the opening quotation mark; it runs to 498. This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. The speech is a deception. 'quae… reddat… solvat' is a relative clause with the subjunctive, 'a way such as will…'. 'gratare' is the imperative of the deponent 'gratari' with the dative 'sorori'; Dido calls herself 'your sister' in the third person. 'eo' is an ablative of separation ('from him'). 'vel' offers the alternative, and either outcome, return or release, suits what she really intends. 'amantem' agrees with 'me'.

sentences.t:
Oceani finem iuxta solemque cadentem
ultimus Aethiopum locus est, ubi maxumus Atlas
axem humero torquet stellis ardentibus aptum:
sentences.l:
Of Ocean the edge beside and the setting sun
the farthest of the Ethiopians place is, where greatest Atlas
the axis on his shoulder turns, fitted with burning stars:
sentences.i: Beside the edge of Ocean and the setting sun lies the farthest place of the Ethiopians, where mighty Atlas turns on his shoulder the axle of heaven, studded with blazing stars:
sentences.n: 'iuxta' follows its two objects, 'finem' and 'solem', 'next to the limit of Ocean and the setting sun'. 'Aethiopum' is a genitive plural in '-um' (the Ethiopians, a people of the far south). 'maxumus' is Greenough's spelling of 'maximus'. 'axem' is the axis of the heavens, which Atlas, the Titan, carries. 'humero' is an ablative of place (the Latin Library has 'umero', the same word). 'aptum' means 'fitted' and agrees with 'axem'; 'stellis ardentibus' says what it is fitted with.

sentences.t:
hinc mihi Massylae gentis monstrata sacerdos,
Hesperidum templi custos, epulasque draconi
quae dabat, et sacros servabat in arbore ramos,
spargens umida mella soporiferumque papaver.
sentences.l:
from there to me of the Massylian race a priestess has been pointed out,
the Hesperides' temple's guardian, and food for the dragon
who gave, and the holy kept in the tree boughs,
sprinkling moist honey and sleep-bringing poppy.
sentences.i: From there a priestess of the Massylian people has been pointed out to me, keeper of the temple of the Hesperides, who used to feed the dragon and guard the holy boughs on the tree, sprinkling moist honey and sleep-bringing poppy.
sentences.n: 'monstrata' is short for 'monstrata est', and 'mihi' is a dative of the agent or interest. The Massylians were a people of north Africa. The Hesperides, nymphs of the far west, guarded the golden apples with a dragon; the priestess takes their part. 'Hesperidum' is a Greek genitive plural in '-um'. 'quae dabat… et servabat' are imperfects of habit, and the relative 'quae' stands after 'epulasque draconi' instead of at the head of its clause. 'draconi' is a dative. 'spargens' is a present participle agreeing with 'sacerdos'. 'soporiferum' (a compound, 'sleep-bearing') agrees with 'papaver'.

sentences.i: She promises that by her charms she can free the minds of whomever she pleases, and send grim cares upon others, halt the water in the rivers, and turn the stars back in their courses;
sentences.n: 'promittit' takes an accusative and infinitive with 'se' as the subject, and four infinitives follow: 'solvere', 'immittere', 'sistere', 'vertere'. 'quas velit' is a subjunctive because it is a subordinate clause inside the report of her claim. 'ast' is the old form of 'at', 'but'. 'aliis' is a dative with 'immittere', 'on others'. 'duras… curas' is the object. 'carminibus' means 'by spells'. Such feats of reversal (stopping rivers, turning stars) are the usual boasts of magic.

sentences.t: nocturnosque movet Manis:
sentences.l: and the nocturnal she stirs Shades:
sentences.i: she stirs the ghosts of the night:
sentences.n: 'Manis' is '-is' for '-es', accusative plural, 'the spirits of the dead', as at 427. 'nocturnos' means 'of night'. 'movet' means 'rouses'. The colon introduces what Anna will see.

sentences.t:
mugire videbis
sub pedibus terram, et descendere montibus ornos.
sentences.l:
to groan you will see
under your feet the earth, and to descend from the mountains ash-trees.
sentences.i: you will see the earth groan beneath your feet, and the ash trees come down from the mountains.
sentences.n: 'videbis' governs two accusatives and infinitives: 'terram mugire' and 'ornos descendere'. 'mugire' is 'bellow, rumble', used of the earth. 'montibus' is an ablative of separation with no preposition, 'from the mountains'. The ash trees walking down from the mountains are a wonder of magic.

sentences.t:
Testor, cara, deos et te, germana, tuumque
dulce caput, magicas invitam accingier artes.
sentences.l:
I call to witness, dear one, the gods and you, sister, and your
sweet head, unwilling to gird myself with magic arts.
sentences.i: I call the gods to witness, dear sister, and you, and your own dear self: it is against my will that I arm myself with magic arts.
sentences.n: 'testor' governs 'deos', 'te' and 'caput', and an accusative and infinitive, 'me… accingier'. 'accingier' is an archaic passive infinitive in '-ier' (= 'accingi') with the middle sense 'to gird oneself'. 'invitam' agrees with the understood 'me', 'unwilling'. 'tuum dulce caput': the head for the person, as at 357 in the last part. 'cara' is a vocative. The Latin Library's 'artis' has the same sense.

sentences.t:
Tu secreta pyram tecto interiore sub auras
erige, et arma viri, thalamo quae fixa reliquit
impius, exuviasque omnis, lectumque iugalem,
quo perii, superimponas:
sentences.l:
You in secret a pyre in the inner house under the open air
build, and the arms of the man, which in the bedchamber fixed he left,
the unholy one, and the spoils all, and the marriage bed,
on which I perished, put on top:
sentences.i: In secret, in the inner part of the house, build a pyre beneath the open sky, and heap upon it the hero's arms, which the traitor left hanging in my chamber, and all his spoils, and the marriage-bed in which I was ruined:
sentences.n: 'secreta' most likely agrees with 'Tu' (feminine nominative), 'in secret'; it could also be read as an adverbial neuter plural. 'tecto interiore' is an ablative of place, 'sub auras' means 'up under the open air' (the pyre rises into the sky). 'erige' is an imperative, and 'superimponas' is a present subjunctive used as a continuing command. 'thalamo quae fixa reliquit' is a relative clause: the arms hung on the bedchamber wall. 'impius' is 'faithless, unholy', and 'exuvias' are the things he put off. 'omnis' is '-is' for '-es'. 'quo perii' is 'on which I perished'. These objects are the pretext of the sympathetic magic.

sentences.t:
abolere nefandi
cuncta viri monumenta iuvat, monstratque sacerdos.”
sentences.l:
to wipe out of the accursed
man all the memorials it pleases, and shows the way the priestess.”
sentences.i: for it is my wish to destroy every memorial of that accursed man, and the priestess directs it.”
sentences.n: The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: Dido's speech ends here. 'iuvat' is impersonal, 'it pleases (me)', and takes the infinitive 'abolere'. 'nefandi viri' is a genitive pair, 'of the unspeakable man'. 'cuncta… monumenta' is the object. 'monstratque sacerdos' is 'and the priestess shows (it)', taking up 'monstrata sacerdos' at 483. 'monumenta' (the Latin Library prints 'monimenta') means 'memorials, reminders'. Her words can be read two ways.

sentences.t: Haec effata silet;
sentences.l: These things having said, she is silent;
sentences.i: With these words she falls silent;
sentences.n: 'Haec effata' is the deponent 'effor' again (cf. 456), a perfect participle with active meaning, 'having spoken'. 'silet' is the present, vivid. A short line of narration like this closes the speech.

sentences.t: pallor simul occupat ora.
sentences.l: pallor at once seizes her face.
sentences.i: and at once a pallor seizes her face.
sentences.n: 'ora' is a neuter plural for the singular, 'her face'. 'simul' means 'at the same time'. 'pallor' betrays what the calm brow (477) hid. 'occupat' means 'takes hold of'.

sentences.t:
Non tamen Anna novis praetexere funera sacris
germanam credit, nec tantos mente furores
concipit, aut graviora timet, quam morte Sychaei:
sentences.l:
Not however Anna with new rites to cloak a funeral
her sister believes, nor so great in her mind frenzies
conceives, or graver things fears, than at the death of Sychaeus:
sentences.i: Anna, however, does not believe that her sister is cloaking a funeral with new rites, nor does she conceive in her mind such madness, nor fear anything graver than at the death of Sychaeus:
sentences.n: 'Non tamen' means 'but not', 'yet not'. 'germanam' is the accusative subject of the infinitive 'praetexere', 'to cloak', after 'credit'; 'funera' (plural) is the object, and 'novis… sacris' an ablative of means. 'nec… concipit' echoes Dido's 'concepit furias' (474). 'graviora' is a comparative neuter plural, 'graver things'. 'quam morte Sychaei' compares Dido's grief now with her grief 'at the death of Sychaeus' (ablative of circumstance), the murder in Book I.

sentences.t: ergo iussa parat.
sentences.l: therefore the orders she prepares.
sentences.i: and so she makes ready what she was told.
sentences.n: 'ergo' marks the consequence. 'iussa' is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, 'the things ordered'. 'parat' is the present, vivid. This is a half-line: at six syllables it cannot be a hexameter, and the poem has other unfinished lines, like 361 and 400 in the last part. The paragraph ends with Anna doing as she is told, not knowing what it is for.
